```suggestion
			if ((ctx->tid_map[i].net == network ||
			     ctx->tid_map[i].net == MCTP_NET_ANY) &&
			    ctx->tid_map[i].eid == eid) {
```

Can we give precedence to exact network matches and use MCTP_NET_ANY only as a fallback?

Both mapping APIs currently exist, so there’s an edge case where callers may use them together. In that case, checking for an exact network match first would avoid wildcard entries (MCTP_NET_ANY) shadowing more specific mappings.

Thanks for the suggestion!
I reworked get_tid() to search in two passes — first for an exact network match, then for MCTP_NET_ANY as a fallback.
Reordering the || operands alone wouldn't change the result since A || B evaluates the same either way, so the two-pass approach felt necessary to properly avoid MCTP_NET_ANY entries shadowing more specific ones.
Does this look reasonable to you?
cool. Your implementation looks cleaner than my suggestion.
Do you think a test case for the edge case I mentioned "Caller calling both API" would be a nice addition?

I've updated the patch with a test that uses both map_tid() and map_tid_fqe() for the same EID and verifies that the exact network match is returned, while a different network still falls back to MCTP_NET_ANY.
Does this cover the scenario you were thinking of?
cool. This looks good.
Verified and work on my platform.
This seems inconsistent. We allow searching with MCTP_NET_ANY (which is 0), but it is blocked here.

I think the two zeros serve different purposes.
The network parameter here comes directly from the kernel when receiving an MCTP packet, and the kernel is expected to fill in the actual device network ID, so 0 shouldn't appear there.
The MCTP_NET_ANY fallback searches stored tid_map entries where map_tid() stores entries with net = 0 to mean "match any network."
Same numeric value, different layers.
@vishnunithyasoundhar.s@intel.com might be able to provide more context since the original network != 0 guard was introduced in [6b8f264].

[6b8f264]: https://github.com/openbmc/libpldm/commit/6b8f2646bc2abbeb7ccb074aa23fb7be929d1f00#diff-1dde80e9a2b9e2874a0aabde1a857d18252904d9c17c31968e4e785836cd3ea4

https://github.com/openbmc/libpldm/blob/80cde632088394b9b3da90cf677b8d2763278c77/src/transport/af-mctp.c#L170

In the linked code, this is the point where we obtain the network value that is later passed to pldm_transport_af_mctp_get_tid. The value comes directly from the kernel MCTP socket, which always provides a valid MCTP link identifier—however, MCTP link IDs are never allowed to be 0.
Therefore, a net = 0 value cannot represent a valid MCTP network.

In scenarios where someone previously used the old API to map a TID:

The network would typically be 1, since that is the default MCTP link ID.
A call to find_tid(..., network, ...) would fail because it would not find a mapping associated with network 1.
A call to find_tid(..., MCTP_NET_ANY, ...) would succeed, assuming the old-API-based mapping still exists, because it searches across all networks.
Acked. Thanks for the information.

That said, I think we can improve the way the split is implemented for the purpose of tests. I've pushed https://gerrit.openbmc.org/c/openbmc/libpldm/+/88342 to demonstrate what I have in mind. Feel free to squash it in if it seems okay.

Hi @andrew@codeconstruct.com.au, I really appreciate the review and the follow-up patch. The concrete example made the intent clear.

I've squashed your changes into patchset 32. The test wrapper files are removed, get_tid() is now marked `LIBPLDM_ABI_TESTING`, and the tests use stack-initialized structs with #if LIBPLDM_API_TESTING guards.

Please take a look when convenient to verify it aligns with your expectations.
